title: Ordered-to-disordered transfer learning with graph neural networks for formation-energy and HOMO-LUMO gap prediction in high-entropy perovskite oxides
authors: Panupol Untarabut, Narjes Jomaa, Sylvian Cadars, Olivier Masson, Samuel Bernard, Assil Bouzid, Santanu Saha
abstract: High-entropy perovskite oxides (HEPOs) represent a chemically complex class of materials with promising functional properties, yet their vast compositional space and, chemical/structural disorder pose significant challenge for accurate property prediction. Graph neural networks (GNNs) enable rapid exploration of materials space but are often limited by the availability of representative training data. Here, we investigate ordered-to-disordered transfer learning using GNNs for formation-energy and HOMO-LUMO gap prediction in HEPOs by transferring knowledge learned from chemically ordered perovskites. Four representative GNN models, including CGCNN, GATGNN, ALIGNN and M3GNet are evaluated to understand the role of structural representations, spanning pairwise two-body and angular three-body interactions in transfer performance. We find strong property-dependent transfer behavior: formation-energy prediction transfers effectively to disordered HEPOs, whereas HOMO-LUMO gap prediction shows limited transferability due to its sensitivity to local chemical environments. Incorporating a small HEPO-specific training dataset substantially improves HOMO-LUMO gap prediction. Representation-level analysis using UMAP further highlights the importance of encoding three-body geometric information such as in ALIGNN for capturing complex structure-property relationships and improving transferability.
summary: This work addresses the challenge of predicting properties in disordered High-Entropy Perovskite Oxides by using graph neural networks trained via transfer learning. The study finds that while structural stability ($	ext{E}_f$) transfers well, electronic gaps ($	ext{E}_g$) require targeted fine-tuning with HEPO data. It highlights that incorporating local geometric information is crucial for accurate modeling of complex disordered materials.
main_problem: Accurately predicting material properties, specifically formation energy and HOMO-LUMO gap, in chemically complex and structurally disordered High-Entropy Perovskite Oxides (HEPOs).
main_result: Knowledge transfer from ordered perovskites is effective for formation energy but fails for the HOMO-LUMO gap due to local environment sensitivity; incorporating small HEPO data significantly improves electronic property prediction.
method: The study employs graph neural networks (GNNs) trained using an ordered-to-disordered transfer learning paradigm, comparing performance across four different GNN architectures.
model_or_system: The physical system is the perovskite oxide structure ($	ext{ABO}_3$), modeled computationally using Special Quasirandom Structures (SQSs) to represent chemical and structural disorder in HEPOs. The prediction targets are DFT-calculated formation energy ($E_f$) and HOMO-LUMO gap ($E_g$).
key_observables: Formation energy ($	ext{E}_f$), HOMO-LUMO gap ($	ext{E}_g$), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and residual distributions.
important_parameters: The transferability of knowledge, the fraction of HEPO-specific training data used for fine-tuning, and the inclusion of three-body geometric information (e.g., bond angles).
main_assumptions: Knowledge learned from chemically ordered perovskites can serve as a starting point for predicting properties in disordered HEPOs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate training loss trajectories showing ALIGNN's superior convergence, and MAE comparisons demonstrating the performance of different models on both ordered and HEPO test sets.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the challenge posed by HEPOs. It then details the methodology using GNNs for transfer learning from ordered to disordered domains. Results are presented by comparing $	ext{E}_f$ vs. $	ext{E}_g$ transferability, followed by an analysis of model performance and optimal data incorporation strategies.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state materials, the core methodology—using advanced ML (GNNs) to extrapolate physical laws from a known, ordered regime to a highly complex, disordered one—is directly relevant to modeling many-body systems where disorder or quenched randomness is present.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Target-property distributions for the training, validation, and test subsets of the ordered single and double perovskite oxide dataset: (a) formation energy (meV/atom) and (b) HOMO-LUMO gap (eV). Formation energy is evaluated with respect to stable binary oxides of different cationic species. Ordered perovskite oxide consists of single ABO3 and double A2BB’O6 perovskites.

Figure 2: Training behavior of the graph neural network models on the training and validation set of the ordered single and double perovskite dataset. (a) Formation-energy(Ef) training and validation loss trajectories for CGCNN, GATGNN, ALIGNN, and M3GNet. (b) HOMO-LUMO gap (Eg) training and validation loss trajectories for the same models. The cyan and pink solid lines represent the training and validation losses, respectively. Grey vertical dashed lines mark the best validation checkpoints.
Figure 3: Train, validation, and test MAE values for the ordered domain (single and double perovskite). (a) Formation-energy error (meV/atom). (b) HOMO-LUMO gap errors (eV).

Figure 4: Prediction quality of the trained GNN models on the ordered single and double perovskite test set. Parity plots for (a) formation-energy and (b) HOMO-LUMO gap predictions. Distribution of the calculated DFT and model predicted values of (c) formation energy and (d) HOMO-LUMO gap. Residual distributions of all GNN models for (e) formation energy and (f) HOMO-LUMO gap.

Figure 5: Chemistry-resolved prediction errors on held out test set of ordered and disordered domain. CGCNN MAE maps for (a) formation energy Ef (meV/atom) and (b) HOMO-LUMO gap Eg (eV). ALIGNN MAE maps for (c) formation energy Ef and (d) HOMO-LUMO gap Eg . Rows denote the A-site element, and columns denote the ordered B-site element or the HEPO transfer group.
